question: The La Rioja biodiversity law was passed in 2023 to protect the region’s environmental assets. After the region’s government changed, the new executive launched a process to modify that law, removing 239 species from the La Rioja list of wild species under special protection and deleting the title on including environmental conservation and restoration across sector-based policies.
The changes are not backed up by any scientific studies to justify reducing protection for those 239 species, which include some at risk of extinction, such as the bearded vulture. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this state of affairs?

What mechanisms does the Commission have in place to ensure that these changes – devoid of any scientific backing – do not undermine the objectives of directives on nature, the protection of endangered species and conservation of native wildlife?

Does the Commission believe that removing cross-cutting provisions on environmental conservation and restoration from sector-based policies is in line with the EU Biodiversity Strategy and the COP15 Global Biodiversity Framework?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2024) 1. The Commission was recently made aware of the ongoing process to modify La Rioja biodiversity law. However, as there is no official information publicly available on the specific changes proposed, the Commission is not yet in a position to assess the situation in detail. 2.

Member States must ensure that any change in their nature legislation at national or regional level is respecting the requirements of the Habitats1 and Birds2 Directives. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is for the competent Spanish authorities to assess if the proposal in question complies with the above-mentioned legal acts. 3.

It is for the Spanish authorities to ensure that national or regional policy is in line with the EU Biodiversity Strategy 20303 and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) adopted at the 15th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).

Spain, as party to the CBD, committed to implement the GBF, including its Target 14 on integrating biodiversity and its multiple values within and across all levels of government and within all sectors.
1 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and

flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 2 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 3 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en
